standard.title: Author's individual style
standard.description: identify and explain characteristics that define an author's individual style
standard.prior_knowledge: Students can recognise that the point of view in a literary text influences how readers interpret and respond to events (AC9E5LE03). They have not yet examined the concept of an individual author's style — the distinctive combination of choices (theme, structure, voice, vocabulary, technique) that characterises a particular author's work across texts.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students can identify and explain characteristics that define an individual author's style, drawing on analysis of multiple texts by the same author.

nodes.label: What constitutes author style
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can name the elements that collectively constitute an author's style — subject/theme, characterisation, text structure, plot development, tone, vocabulary, voice, grammatical structures, and visual techniques.
nodes.minimum_width: Name at least four elements that can characterise an author's style; identify examples of two of these elements in a provided text extract.
nodes.typical_width: Examine a text and identify examples of the full range of style elements: subject, theme, characterisation, text structure, plot development, tone, vocabulary, voice, grammatical structures, and visual techniques; discuss which elements seem most defining for a given author.
wider: Compare a list of style elements for two contrasting authors and analyse which elements are universal and which are distinctive
Investigate how illustrators also develop individual styles in picture books — identifying characteristic visual features across multiple works
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who cannot name and identify the style element vocabulary cannot perform the cross-text pattern recognition required in Node 2 — they have no analytical categories to apply.

response_modes.reason: Students need to encounter the full range of style elements across multiple texts before the concept of 'style as a pattern across texts' becomes visible. A single text only shows one data point; style emerges from accumulation.

success_criteria: Names at least four elements that constitute author style
Identifies at least two style elements in a provided text extract with evidence

nodes.label: Style as a cross-text pattern
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can identify similarities across two or more texts by the same author that define the qualities characterising that author's style.
nodes.minimum_width: Identify at least two similarities across two texts by the same author and explain what these reveal about the author's characteristic style.
nodes.typical_width: Explore two or more texts by the same author; identify similarities in subject, theme, characterisation, structure, plot, tone, vocabulary, voice and grammatical structures; articulate the qualities that characterise the author's individual style.
wider: Explore two or more texts by a First Nations Australian author and identify characteristic elements of their writing, including images, themes and language choices
Compare illustrations across two or more picture books by the same illustrator and identify the characteristic visual features that define their style
nodes.hinge_reason: Without cross-text pattern recognition, Node 3's explanatory task has no data — students cannot explain a style they have not identified across texts.

response_modes.reason: The concept of style as a cross-text pattern is invisible with a single text. Reading two texts by the same author is the minimum for identifying style — reading more texts (and different authors) strengthens the concept by showing what persists vs. what varies.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: Exploring First Nations Australian authors' characteristic styles is both required and rich — it builds cultural knowledge alongside literary analysis skills and develops students' ability to engage with diverse literary traditions.
success_criteria: Identifies at least two characteristics that appear across two or more texts by the same author
Names these as defining features of the author's style, not just features of a single text

nodes.label: Explaining style choices
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can explain the characteristics that define a specific author's individual style using literary metalanguage.
nodes.minimum_width: Write or speak a brief explanation of one author's style, using at least three style elements with textual evidence.
nodes.typical_width: Produce an explanation of an author's individual style that identifies multiple characteristic elements with specific textual evidence; discuss how these choices create the author's distinctive voice and effect on readers.
wider: Compare the defining style features of two authors who write in the same genre and explain what makes each distinctive
Write a short piece in the style of a chosen author, then annotate the choices made to reflect the style elements identified

response_modes.reason: Producing an explanation of an author's style integrates knowledge of style elements (Node 1) with cross-text pattern recognition (Node 2) into a coherent explanatory act — the components come together in the writer's own analytical production.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: Writing in an author's style is rich creative/analytical integration — students must have genuinely understood the style elements to imitate them deliberately, and this produces authentic evidence of learning.
success_criteria: Identifies and names at least three style elements with specific textual evidence from the author's work
Explains how these elements work together to create the author's distinctive style
